biography.text: This focused entry examines one bounded passage and the organization of the Canon; it is not a complete biography of Ibn Sīnā.
gaps: Build a sourced biography from Arabic biographical sources and specialist studies; reconcile chronology and political context.

timeline.text: Basim Musallam's Encyclopaedia Iranica article states that Book I of the Canon was composed before 405/1015. This gives a terminus ante quem for Book I, not a date for the whole work or a manuscript copy.
gaps: Verify the chronology against primary biographical evidence and specialist studies.

fields.text: This batch studies the Canon's opening definition of medicine and its boundary with natural philosophy as reported by Iranica and in O. Cameron Gruner's 1930 English rendering of Book I. Gruner's text is a historical translation mediated through Latin editions, not a new translation or direct collation of the Arabic.
gaps: Collate the Arabic text with a modern Arabic edition and Mazhar H. Shah's translation, checking each cited passage against its Arabic wording and page layout.
Develop separate investigations of the Canon's pharmacology, clinical reasoning, and the Shifāʾ without importing modern medical claims.

legacy.text: Iranica describes the Canon as an influential and systematic exposition of Galenic medicine, while explicitly cautioning that it was neither the first Arabic systematic medical work nor unique in its kind. This dossier makes no absolute priority claim.
gaps: Trace particular translations, editions, teaching contexts, and transmission claims through specialist scholarship rather than inferring influence from later fame.

sources.title: Avicenna x. Medicine and Biology
sources.authorOrInstitution: Basim Musallam, Encyclopaedia Iranica, vol. III, fasc. 1, pp. 94–99
sources.notes: Read the article sections on the Canon, its five-book structure, medicine's scope, and the Aristotle-Galen relationship. It reports the opening definition and historical context. Iranica also notes that the Canon has not been critically edited and that Gruner's English version is based on the Latin translation with departures from Arabic; use this as scholarly synthesis, not as a primary Arabic edition.

sources.title: A Treatise on the Canon of Medicine of Avicenna, Incorporating a Translation of the First Book
sources.notes: Consulted the digitized Book I OCR and its stated bibliographic basis. Gruner's translation was made from the Latin version and informed by study of the 1593 Rome Arabic edition and later printings; it is therefore a mediated historical translation. The OCR is not an Arabic manuscript image and can contain recognition errors. The bounded passage is the opening definition/scope discussion in Book I, Preliminary Remarks, printed pp. 25–27 in the 1930 edition.

sources.title: The Canon of Medicine, Book I (digital text)
sources.authorOrInstitution: Classics Library, transcription of O. Cameron Gruner's 1930 translation
sources.notes: Used to inspect the OCR transcription and identify the underlying 1930 edition. This is not an independent translation or an Arabic witness; the host describes it as OCR text and says front matter and appendices are omitted.

sources.title: The General Principles of Avicenna's Canon of Medicine
sources.notes: Iranica identifies this as a more recent translation of Book I and notes that it includes anatomy omitted by Gruner. The translation itself was not consulted in this batch; it is a priority for future comparison.

works.subject: A five-book medical compendium
works.purpose: The opening of Book I defines medicine's subject and distinguishes it from the theoretical inquiry assigned to natural philosophy, while the work arranges general principles, drugs, organ-specific diseases, general conditions, and compound remedies into five books.
works.date: Book I composed before 405/1015 according to Musallam; this is not a date for every part or a surviving copy.

passages.editionOrShelfmark: O. Cameron Gruner, 1930 translation of Book I; OCR transcription
passages.language: English translation from Latin, with Arabic editions consulted by Gruner
passages.originalPassage: Medicine is described as knowledge of the body's states in health and illness, directed toward preserving health or restoring it. The opening discussion then distinguishes medicine's practical domain from questions about the first principles of natural philosophy.
passages.translation: Paraphrase of Gruner's English rendering; not a direct translation from Arabic.
passages.printedPage: 1930 ed., pp. 25–27 (opening definition and scope discussion; verify against page images)
passages.chapterOrSection: Book I, Preliminary Remarks, definition and scope of medicine
passages.explanation: This records the bounded argument as represented in a historical translation and independently summarized by Iranica. Gruner's wording, Latin intermediary, OCR, and the absence of Arabic collation limit textual precision; no current medical advice or efficacy claim follows from this passage.

works.notes: Iranica says the Canon is not unique and was not the first systematic Arabic medical work; earlier works include those of al-Rāzī and ʿAlī ibn ʿAbbās al-Majūsī. Do not convert later authority into an invention-priority claim.

investigations.title: Defining medicine's scope in the opening of the Canon
investigations.field: History of medicine / philosophy of science
investigations.historicalProblem: How does the Canon's opening define medicine, and how does it delimit medical inquiry from natural philosophy?
investigations.historicalContext: Musallam situates Ibn Sīnā's medical writing within longstanding Galenic medicine and its disagreements with Aristotelian natural philosophy. The Canon synthesizes these traditions; its authority should not erase earlier Arabic medical scholarship or make its historical physiology equivalent to modern science.
investigations.method: Read Musallam's Iranica account and the opening scope discussion as printed in Gruner's 1930 English Book I transcription. Used the host transcription to identify sections, then recorded Gruner's mediation and OCR limitations. No Arabic manuscript or critical edition was collated; Shah's 1966 translation is recorded as a future comparison, not as consulted evidence.
investigations.observationsOrCalculations: The sources describe a bounded division of labor: medicine studies bodily conditions in health and illness for preservation or restoration, while foundational questions about elements, humors, and faculties are assigned to natural philosophy. Iranica reports a five-book arrangement: general principles; simple drugs; diseases of individual organs; conditions affecting the whole body or any part; and compound medicines.
investigations.reportedResult: The evidence supports a cautious account of the Canon's declared disciplinary scope and editorial organization. It does not establish that the boundary was consistently maintained in practice or that this historical framework is medically valid today.
investigations.whatWasNew: This dossier adds a source-linked, reviewable passage record and makes the translation chain explicit. It does not claim a new medical discovery, the first Arabic medical system, or a unique Canon structure.
investigations.limitations: The passage is represented through Gruner's 1930 English version, based on Latin, and an OCR transcription; no fresh translation from Arabic was made. Iranica says the Canon lacks a critical edition and notes departures in the Latin-derived Gruner text. Arabic page alignment, variants, manuscript witnesses, and Shah's translation remain to be checked. This is historical research, not medical advice.
investigations.laterInfluence: Not assessed in this bounded batch; influence requires evidence from specific translations, teaching records, and citations.

claims.locator: Iranica, section 'Medicine and natural philosophy'; discussion of Canon I, first sentence
claims.uncertainty: This is a modern scholar's English rendering; Arabic wording and edition variants were not collated here.

claims.text: Musallam describes Ibn Sīnā as using Canon I's opening chapter to distinguish medicine's domain from foundational questions assigned to natural philosophy.
claims.locator: Iranica, 'Medicine and natural philosophy'; Gruner 1930, Book I, Preliminary Remarks, pp. 25–27
claims.uncertainty: The textual formulation relies on a Latin-mediated translation; direct Arabic comparison is outstanding.

claims.text: Musallam characterizes the Canon as a major exposition of Galenic medicine and explains Ibn Sīnā's effort to reconcile Galenic evidence with Aristotelian theoretical commitments.
claims.uncertainty: This is the article's scholarly interpretation of a complex corpus, not a claim that the traditions were fully reconciled.

claims.text: Iranica describes five Canon books covering general principles, simple drugs, diseases of individual organs, general conditions, and compound medicines.
claims.uncertainty: This high-level modern outline is not a collation of every section or edition.

claims.text: Musallam states that Book I of the Canon was composed before 405/1015.
claims.uncertainty: Reported chronology; no independent primary-source verification in this batch, and it should not be extended to a manuscript copy date.
